prompt: Which three features separate social stratification from mere differences between individuals?
options: It is structured, persistent and inherited
It is voluntary, temporary and individual
It is biological, fixed and universal
It is written in law and enforced by courts
correctAnswer: It is structured, persistent and inherited
explanation: Stratification is attached to positions rather than personal quirks, lasts for decades, and passes from parents to children. It need not be written in law: class systems are stratified without any legal ranks.

prompt: An achieved status is one that comes with birth, such as a noble title.
explanation: That describes an ascribed status. An achieved status is won through effort, skill or luck, such as a medical degree or an election victory. Real societies mix both kinds.

prompt: What did the Pew Research Center's 2019 to 2020 survey of 29,999 Indian adults find about caste?
options: Nearly all Indians identify with a caste, whatever their religion
Only Hindus still identify with a caste
Most Indians say they belong to the Brahmin caste
Caste identity has largely disappeared from Indian social life
correctAnswer: Nearly all Indians identify with a caste, whatever their religion
explanation: Many people assume caste is a purely Hindu matter, but Pew found that nearly all Indians identify with a caste regardless of religion. Only 4% said they were Brahmin, and caste still shapes friendships and attitudes to marriage.

prompt: Match each stratification system or ideal to its basis:

pairs.right: Ritual purity and hereditary closure rules
Legal orders with different rights and tax burdens
Position in the economy, formally open to all
Positions allocated by talent and effort

explanation: Caste ranks hereditary groups by ritual purity and forbids intermarriage; estates were legal orders such as France's clergy, nobility and commons; class rests on economic position with no legal barriers; meritocracy is the ideal of allocating positions by merit.

prompt: In pre-revolutionary France the clergy, the nobility and the commons formed three legal orders known as _____.
explanation: France's estates were legal orders. The clergy and nobility were largely exempt from tax, while the Third Estate, somewhere between 90% and 98% of the population, carried most of the burden.

prompt: Michael Young introduced the word "meritocracy" in 1958 as praise for a society that rewards talent and effort.
explanation: Young's 1958 book was a satire, and his feelings about the idea were mixed. The word had already appeared in print two years earlier, and for the left-leaning English academics who used it, it carried a negative connotation.

prompt: Find the error in this reasoning about class societies:
steps: Caste systems use closure rules that forbid marriage and mobility between castes.
Estate systems fix positions in law, as France's three orders did before 1789.
Class systems replaced legal orders with economic groups and formally meritocratic processes.
Since no law assigns anyone a class, class position in modern societies no longer passes from parents to children.
The English life-expectancy gap by deprivation shows that formal openness can coexist with large, patterned inequality.
explanation: Step 4 confuses formally open with equally open. Class systems have no legal barriers, but class position is still strongly inherited, as later lessons on mobility and the transmission of advantage show.

prompt: In 1789 the Third Estate had 578 deputies, against 303 for the clergy and 282 for the nobility. Why could it still lose?
options: If each estate voted as a bloc, the two privileged orders could outvote it two to one
Only nobles were allowed to vote in the Estates-General
Its deputies were outnumbered by the clergy's
The king had abolished the Estates-General before it met
correctAnswer: If each estate voted as a bloc, the two privileged orders could outvote it two to one
explanation: Under the 1614 rule each estate had one vote, so clergy and nobility together could always outvote the commons whatever their numbers. The dispute ended with the Third Estate forming a National Assembly.

prompt: For Karl Marx, what defines a person's class?
options: Their relationship to the means of production
Their lifestyle and social honour
Their level of education
The political party they support
correctAnswer: Their relationship to the means of production
explanation: Marx's basic cleavage runs between capitalists, who own productive property, and workers, who must sell their labour power. Lifestyle and honour belong to Weber's status groups, and organised power to his parties.

prompt: Davis and Moore described stratification as an unconsciously evolved device rather than a system designed by an elite.
explanation: Their 1945 argument held that unequal rewards evolved, without anyone planning them, as a way to ensure that important positions are conscientiously filled by the most qualified people.

prompt: Match each concept to its meaning:

pairs.right: Market situation: what you can sell and how scarce it is
A community sharing a style of life and social honour
Organised power, from parties to pressure groups
Managers and professionals who sell labour yet control work

explanation: Weber split stratification into class, status and party. Erik Olin Wright added contradictory class locations to Marx's scheme for people such as managers, who have authority over workers, and semi-autonomous professionals.

prompt: Which objection by Melvin Tumin did the most damage to the Davis-Moore theory?
options: Stratification itself limits the discovery of talent, because children born at the bottom may never be trained
No society has any jobs that are more important than others
In practice every job is paid the same
Inequality first appeared in industrial societies
correctAnswer: Stratification itself limits the discovery of talent, because children born at the bottom may never be trained
explanation: Tumin argued that a stratified society wastes talent, so differential rewards could only be justified as functional where everyone with potential has genuinely equal access to recruitment and training.

prompt: Weber's term for the process by which groups devise and enforce membership rules to improve their position by monopolistic tactics is social _____.
explanation: Social closure explains how groups protect their rewards. Frank Parkin argued in 1979 that exclusionary rules let closed groups maximise their claims to rewards and opportunities.

prompt: If a job is highly paid, that alone shows, on Davis and Moore's own terms, that it is functionally important.
explanation: Many people assume high pay simply reflects importance. Critics call that reasoning circular: the theory labels the best-rewarded roles the most important and then cites their rewards as proof. A 1959 critique added that powerful incumbents can demand more than motivation requires.

prompt: In Kleiner and Krueger's 2009 survey, licensed workers earned about 14% more. What can that finding tell you on its own?
options: That licensing is associated with a wage premium, but not how much of it rewards quality and how much reflects closure
That the whole premium is a closure rent
That licensing lowers wages
That licensing has no link to wages
correctAnswer: That licensing is associated with a wage premium, but not how much of it rewards quality and how much reflects closure
explanation: Defenders say licensing protects the public, so part of the premium may reward quality; closure theorists say entry requirements shrink supply and push up pay. The data show the premium but cannot split it between the two.

prompt: Find the error in this summary of the Davis-Moore argument:
steps: Every society must motivate able people to fill important and difficult jobs.
Its solution is a hierarchy of unequal rewards attached to positions.
The argument justifies unequal positions, not unequal starting points.
The theory therefore specifies exactly how much inequality a society needs.
Tumin replied that rewards are only justified as functional where access to training is genuinely equal.
explanation: Davis and Moore never said how much inequality is enough. That gap let critics argue that real societies may have far more inequality than any motivational problem requires.

prompt: What does the Goldthorpe schema classify people by?
options: The kind of employment relationship their job involves
Their annual income alone
Their tastes in music and food
Their parents' religion
correctAnswer: The kind of employment relationship their job involves
explanation: The Goldthorpe schema is Weberian in spirit and sorts jobs by employment relations, chiefly the contrast between a service relationship and a labour contract, rather than by income or prestige.

prompt: The NS-SEC classifies positions rather than people.
explanation: Two people in the same job on the same kind of contract land in the same NS-SEC class, whatever their accent, savings or taste. The classification describes positions in the labour market.

prompt: Match each term to its description:

pairs.right: Salary plus long-term prospects such as security and a career
A wage for discrete amounts of work or time
Jobs that mix features of both
Never worked and long-term unemployed

explanation: The service relationship typifies class 1, the labour contract typifies class 7, and intermediate forms mix the two. Class 8 covers people with no employment relationship at all.

prompt: In Census 2021 for England and Wales, which NS-SEC class was the largest?
options: Lower managerial, administrative and professional occupations
Routine occupations
Higher managerial, administrative and professional occupations
Small employers and own account workers
correctAnswer: Lower managerial, administrative and professional occupations
explanation: Class 2 held 19.9% of usual residents aged 16 and over (9.7 million people). Class 1 held 13.1%, routine occupations 12.1%, and small employers and own account workers 10.6%.

prompt: The Great British Class Survey called its poorest and most deprived class the _____.
explanation: The precariat, or precarious proletariat, made up 15% of the population in the survey's model. Supporters argued it, and the elite, had been missed by conventional class analysis.

prompt: Because more than 161,000 people took part, the Great British Class Survey's seven classes rest on a large, representative sample.
explanation: Size is not representativeness. The web respondents were self-selected and mostly well educated, so the classes came from a model estimated almost entirely on a GfK quota sample of 1,026 people, as Colin Mills pointed out.

prompt: What was Colin Mills's objection about what the Great British Class Survey's classes could explain?
options: Cultural and social capital were built into the definition of the classes, so the classes cannot explain differences in those capitals
The survey asked no questions about income or savings
The classes were defined by occupation alone
The survey left out the elite
correctAnswer: Cultural and social capital were built into the definition of the classes, so the classes cannot explain differences in those capitals
explanation: Goldthorpe's tradition defines class by employment relations and then tests what class predicts. Building capitals into the definition makes any link between class and those capitals true by construction.

prompt: Put the steps by which the Great British Class Survey produced its seven classes in order:
steps: BBC Lab UK launches an online questionnaire in January 2011
More than 161,000 self-selected people respond, mostly well educated
A second, identical survey is run with GfK on a quota sample
A latent profile model is estimated, almost entirely on the GfK sample
Seven classes, from elite to precariat, are announced in 2013
explanation: The web survey came first, but its skew towards well-educated respondents led the team to run the GfK survey. The model behind the seven classes rested almost entirely on that smaller sample of 1,026.

prompt: Which of these is a stock rather than a flow?
options: Wealth: what you own minus your debts
Your annual salary
Monthly benefit payments
Interest received this year
correctAnswer: Wealth: what you own minus your debts
explanation: Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock held at a moment. A newly qualified doctor can have high income and negative wealth.

prompt: In Great Britain, income is distributed more unequally than wealth.
explanation: It is the other way round. The ONS put the Gini coefficient for income at 0.36 in 2020 and for wealth at around 0.6, because wealth accumulates over a lifetime and can be inherited.

prompt: Between April 2018 and March 2020, the wealthiest 10% of households in Great Britain held _____% of all the wealth.
explanation: The wealthiest 10% held 43% of household wealth, while the bottom 50% held only 9%.

prompt: Why do sociologists treat a single Gini coefficient with caution?
options: Two very different distributions can share the same Gini, and it is relatively insensitive to the very top
It can take values above 1
It measures wealth but never income
It ignores everyone below the median
correctAnswer: Two very different distributions can share the same Gini, and it is relatively insensitive to the very top
explanation: A Gini squeezes a whole distribution into one number between 0 and 1. That is why researchers add top income shares, which showed that the post-1980 rise in American inequality was concentrated at the very top.

prompt: Match each study to its finding:

pairs.right: U-shaped US top income shares, 1913 to 1998
Bottom half's pre-tax income stagnant at about $16,000
Top shares lower and rising less; after-tax shares little changed
r minus g does not explain historical top shares

explanation: Top-share research began with tax returns, moved to distributional national accounts, and now faces challenges both on measurement (Auten and Splinter) and on theory (Acemoglu and Robinson).

prompt: Piketty and Saez built their long-run series of US top income shares mainly from individual tax returns.
explanation: Surveys capture few very rich people, so Piketty and Saez used tax returns back to 1913, finding a U-shaped pattern over the century.

prompt: Find the error in this argument about wealth inequality:
steps: Wealth accumulates over a lifetime, so older households tend to be richer.
The ONS found median wealth was highest for households headed by someone aged 55 to State Pension age.
So even a society with no classes would show young people looking poorer than people near retirement.
Therefore age fully explains wealth inequality, and parents' wealth tells you nothing about their children's.
explanation: Age explains part of the gap but not all of it. Parents' wealth predicts their adult children's wealth: the Social Mobility Commission found that a 10% increase in parents' wealth goes with a 2.9% increase for sons and 3.8% for daughters.

prompt: What is the fairest summary of the dispute between Auten and Splinter and Piketty, Saez and Zucman?
options: Both try to capture income that tax returns miss, but they reach different answers about how much US top shares rose
One side denies that top shares fell in the mid-twentieth century
They disagree about whether the United States taxes income at all
Both agree that after-tax top shares have tripled since 1980
correctAnswer: Both try to capture income that tax returns miss, but they reach different answers about how much US top shares rose
explanation: Few researchers doubt the broad shape of a mid-century fall and a rise after 1980. The argument is over its size, over the effect of taxes and transfers, and over whether r greater than g explains anything.

prompt: What does relative mobility measure?
options: How much your starting point affects your chances compared with people from other origins
How many people earn more than their parents
How often people move house
How fast the economy grows
correctAnswer: How much your starting point affects your chances compared with people from other origins
explanation: Absolute mobility counts how many people move up or down. Relative mobility compares the chances of people from different origins, usually with odds ratios.

prompt: If an economy creates many more professional jobs, lots of working-class children can rise even if relative mobility stays the same.
explanation: This is structural mobility. Britain's surplus of upward over downward mobility reflects increasing room at the top as the occupational structure changed.

prompt: What did Raj Chetty and colleagues find about US mobility from tax records?
options: Absolute mobility fell from about 90% to 50%, while rank-based relative mobility stayed stable for people born 1971 to 1993
Both absolute and relative mobility collapsed after 1970
Absolute mobility rose while relative mobility fell
Neither has changed since 1940
correctAnswer: Absolute mobility fell from about 90% to 50%, while rank-based relative mobility stayed stable for people born 1971 to 1993
explanation: A common belief is that relative mobility has collapsed. The tax data say otherwise: the chance of climbing the rankings held steady, while the share of children out-earning their parents fell because more growth went to the top.

prompt: Alan Krueger named the cross-country link between high inequality and low intergenerational mobility the Great _____ Curve.
explanation: Krueger presented the Great Gatsby Curve in January 2012, building on Miles Corak's work: more unequal countries show more persistence of income from one generation to the next.

prompt: Match each mobility term to its meaning:

pairs.right: Share of people better or worse off than their parents
How much origin shapes chances compared with others
Movement produced by changes in the job structure
Ratio of two groups' odds of reaching rather than avoiding an outcome

explanation: Absolute and relative mobility answer different questions, and structural change can raise absolute mobility without changing relative chances. Odds ratios are the standard measure of relative mobility.

prompt: Krueger's 2012 data confirmed the old belief that the United States is especially mobile compared with other developed countries.
explanation: Early twentieth-century scholars thought so, and Werner Sombart even blamed American mobility for weak socialist parties. Krueger's data showed the reverse: parental income matters more for children's success in the US than in other developed economies.

prompt: Chetty's team found that faster GDP growth alone could not restore 1940s rates of absolute mobility. What would reverse more than 70% of the decline?
options: Spreading growth across income groups as evenly as it was for the 1940 birth cohort
Doubling the rate of GDP growth
Cutting inflation to zero
Raising the school-leaving age
correctAnswer: Spreading growth across income groups as evenly as it was for the 1940 birth cohort
explanation: Absolute mobility fell mainly because more growth went to the top, not because growth slowed. A more equal distribution of growth would undo most of the decline.

prompt: Put these steps in order to calculate the Social Mobility Commission's odds ratio for homeownership:
steps: Note that 71% of homeowners' children own and 29% rent
Compute their odds of owning: 71 divided by 29, about 2.45
Note that 46% of renters' children own and 54% rent
Compute their odds of owning: 46 divided by 54, about 0.85
Divide the first odds by the second to get an odds ratio of about 2.9
explanation: An odds ratio uses all four percentages. The children of owners had nearly three times the odds of owning rather than renting; if more renters' children became owners, the ratio would fall.

prompt: What did Annette Lareau call the middle-class style of child-rearing built on organised activities designed to develop children's talents?
options: Concerted cultivation
The accomplishment of natural growth
Habitus
Status attainment
explanation: Lareau contrasted concerted cultivation with the accomplishment of natural growth, in which development unfolds spontaneously once comfort, food and shelter are provided.

prompt: Lareau found that the split between the two child-rearing styles ran mainly along racial lines.
explanation: The split ran along class lines. Middle-class parents, whether Black or white, practised concerted cultivation; working-class and poor families relied on the accomplishment of natural growth.

prompt: According to Elitist Britain 2019, what share of the elite group as a whole had been privately educated?
options: 39%, more than five times the 7% of the population
7%, the same as the population
65%, like senior judges
90%, almost all of them
correctAnswer: 39%, more than five times the 7% of the population
explanation: Two fifths of the more than 5,000 people studied were privately educated. Senior judges were the most concentrated group, at 65% privately educated and 71% Oxbridge.

prompt: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.right: Organised activities designed to draw out talents
Development left to unfold once basic needs are met
Upwardly mobile professionals earning less than privileged peers
Pairing with partners like yourself in education and earnings

explanation: These are four routes by which advantage is passed on or limited: child-rearing, the pay of the upwardly mobile, and who marries whom.

prompt: Chetty, Deming and Friedman found that children from the top 1% were more than _____ as likely as middle-class children with comparable test scores to attend an Ivy-Plus college.
explanation: Two thirds of the gap came from higher admission rates at equal scores, driven by alumni preferences, non-academic credentials and athletic recruitment.

prompt: After correcting their figures, Greenwood and colleagues found that matching US couples at random in 2005 would cut the household-income Gini from 0.43 to 0.34.
explanation: That was the original, widely repeated claim. Their 2015 corrigendum showed random matching lowers the Gini only from 0.430 to 0.420, a small effect; the rise in single and divorced households mattered more.

prompt: Which three factors drove the admissions advantage of high-income applicants at Ivy-Plus colleges?
options: Preferences for alumni children, weight on non-academic credentials, and athletic recruitment
Higher test scores, better essays and more advanced courses
Region, race and gender quotas
Early application, interviews and tuition discounts
correctAnswer: Preferences for alumni children, weight on non-academic credentials, and athletic recruitment
explanation: These three factors were uncorrelated or negatively correlated with success after college, while test scores strongly predicted it. Flagship public universities showed no such advantage for the rich.

prompt: Find the error in this summary of the class ceiling study:
steps: Laurison and Friedman used the Panel Study of Income Dynamics to link childhood class to adult jobs and earnings.
Upwardly mobile people in high-status US occupations earned almost $20,000 a year less than colleagues from privileged backgrounds.
Fewer college degrees explain part of that gap.
Once education, race and other predictors of earnings are accounted for, the gap disappears.
The gap was largest among white people and is distinct from the racial pay gap.
explanation: A substantial gap of around $11,700 a year remains after accounting for education, race and other predictors. Reaching a top job does not erase class origin.

prompt: How did Mollie Orshansky set the original US poverty thresholds in the mid-1960s?
options: The cost of a minimum food diet multiplied by three
60% of median household income
$1 a day in 1985 prices
A public vote on which items are necessities
correctAnswer: The cost of a minimum food diet multiplied by three
explanation: The multiplier covered other family expenses. The official measure is still used: in 2024 the official poverty rate was 10.6%, or 35.9 million people.

prompt: In UK statistics, a household is in relative low income if its income, adjusted for household size, is below 60% of that year's median.
explanation: This relative line moves with the society. In the financial year ending 2024, 17% of people were below it before housing costs and 21% after.

prompt: The World Bank's June 2025 update raised its estimate of people in extreme poverty in 2022 by about 125 million. Why?
options: A higher line, reflecting better data on consumption and the cost of basic needs in low-income countries
Living standards in poor countries suddenly collapsed
The Bank switched to a relative poverty line
The Bank began counting people in rich countries
correctAnswer: A higher line, reflecting better data on consumption and the cost of basic needs in low-income countries
explanation: The world did not suddenly get poorer. Improved household surveys captured consumption more fully, countries raised their national lines, and the international line, set from low-income countries' lines, rose to $3.00.

prompt: The 1983 Breadline Britain survey pioneered the _____ method of measuring poverty, which counts households that cannot afford items most people regard as necessities.
explanation: Under the consensual method an item counts as a necessity if a majority says so, and an enforced lack of three or more necessities is taken as a measure of deprivation poverty.

prompt: Match each international poverty line to its description:

pairs.right: First line, in 1985 prices, from six very poor countries
2022 line in 2017 PPPs, median of 28 low-income countries
June 2025 line in 2021 PPPs, rounded from $3.04
Higher line for upper-middle-income countries

explanation: The method has stayed the same since 1990, measuring absolute poverty by the standards of the poorest countries, while prices and data have been updated. Higher lines serve middle-income countries.

prompt: Britain's "absolute" low-income measure is anchored to 60% of the median for the financial year ending 2011, adjusted for inflation.
explanation: So even the absolute measure is relative underneath: it fixes a past relative line and holds it constant in real terms.

prompt: Which of these was NOT one of Adam Corlett's 2016 criticisms of the elephant curve?
options: The surveys left China out entirely
The set of countries in the data changed between 1988 and 2008
Faster population growth in poorer countries dragged down measured growth around the 70th to 85th percentiles
Weak rich-country figures were driven by Japan and by former Soviet satellites
correctAnswer: The surveys left China out entirely
explanation: China was central to the curve: its rise from the bottom ranks created the global middle. Corlett's points were about changing country coverage, uneven population growth and the influence of Japan and Eastern Europe.

prompt: Find the error in this account of the elephant curve debate:
steps: Lakner and Milanovic found the biggest winners of 1988 to 2008 near the global median, 90% of them in Asia.
The apparent losers sat around the 85th percentile, almost 90% of them in mature economies.
Corlett found that holding the set of countries constant raised measured global growth from 24% to 32%.
Leaving out Japan and former Soviet satellites, the other mature economies' average real incomes grew 52%.
The World Inequality Report 2018 therefore concluded that the elephant curve had disappeared.
explanation: The World Inequality Report 2018 found the elephant even more marked, with the global top 1% capturing 27% of total growth from 1980 to 2016. The debate is still open.
